data.title: Opec+ set to keep oil production targets steady, sources say
data.description:
[MOSCOW/LONDON] Opec+ oil producers are set to keep first-quarter 2027 output targets unchanged at their Sunday (Nov 29) meeting, three sources told Reuters, with uncertainty over the Iran war and disagreements over capacity estimates clouding discussions.

Opec+ includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia.

The group had planned to use the findings of its first-ever review of members’ production capacity to help set 2027 targets at Sunday’s meeting, although disputes over some estimates have complicated those discussions.

The group has an agreement in principle to keep output targets unchanged in the first quarter of 2027, the people said. Oil ministers are set to hold a series of four meetings on Sunday.

Oil analyst firm Rapidan Energy Group also expects no changes to production targets, citing uncertainty over the duration of the Iran war and its effect on crude output and exports.

The capacity review has become a source of tension among some members. Iraq is dissatisfied with preliminary findings that assessed its production capacity at 4.9 million barrels per day, while Kazakhstan is also seeking a higher estimate, sources told Reuters earlier this week.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Wednesday the group would complete the capacity review by the end of 2026, and ministers on Sunday would see what stage the review was at.

Forecasts of oil surplus weigh on market

Rystad Energy forecasts a global oil surplus of about five million barrels per day in 2027, equivalent to roughly 5 per cent of worldwide demand, even if Gulf supplies recover only partially.

The outlook underscores the pressure on Opec+ as it weighs production policy for 2027.

Sunday’s meeting comes months after the United Arab Emirates left Opec and Opec+ in order to pump more oil after years of arguing that its quota did not reflect its investment in capacity.

Angola quit Opec at the start of 2024, and Iraq has warned it may leave if its quota is not raised. REUTERS

data.title: European shares rise on tech, miners strength; head for weekly gains despite US tariff proposals
data.description:
THE EUROPEAN share benchmark rose on Friday (Nov 27), with miners and technology stocks leading gains, as investors prepared to end the week strong despite new US tariff proposals and the prospect of higher interest rates.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 joined global stock markets that rose sharply following a US holiday lull that gave some respite from artificial intelligence jitters.

The benchmark gained 1 per cent to 643.52 points by 0933 GMT, its highest level in a week and its sharpest gain since mid-May.

For the week, it was up nearly 3 per cent, bouncing from the steepest weekly decline since late March 2025 posted last week.

“There doesn’t seem to be any firm catalyst behind the bounce that we’ve seen, but it has been a very bruising month. What we’re seeing here is dip buyers coming in,” said Fiona Cincotta, senior market analyst at StoneX.

European technology stocks added 2.6 per cent on Friday, led by semiconductor shares ASML, ASM International and Infineon, which gained between 5 per cent and 6 per cent. For the week, the index was 1 per cent higher.

Mining stocks jumped more than 4 per cent as copper and gold prices rose. Fresnillo and Pan African Resources rose more than 6 per cent each.

Defence stocks rose, with Rheinmetall up 4.2 per cent after a report on a planned AI-platform partnership with Deutsche Telekom.

The broader aerospace and defence index gained 2 per cent after Bloomberg News reported the EU was planning new funds to replace the US war-fighting capabilities.

Investors, meanwhile, shrugged off the Trump administration’s move to propose tariffs on goods from the EU.

“The market has a lot of other worries that it’s been pricing in. I don’t think it is seeing tariffs as a major headwind,” Cincotta said.

Consumer-facing foods and beverages and personal and household goods were among the weakest performers, with sportswear makers Adidas and Puma down around 1.4 per cent and 1.3 per cent, respectively.

Data this week showed US inflation rose further in October, and the economy grew more than previously expected, adding to bets on interest rate hikes.

Markets await Sunday’s snap election in Spain, called by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez after parliament rejected housing measures aimed at tackling a crisis that has triggered protests across the country.

Among other individual stocks, Thales gained 2 per cent after French laser technology company Lumibird said it had entered exclusive talks to sell a controlling stake to the defence group. Lumibird surged 18.5 per cent. REUTERS

data.title: Firms look for creative problem-solving, relationship-building skills in AI era: panel
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] As artificial intelligence tools become more capable of retrieving information and handling routine tasks, employers are shifting their gaze towards skills that algorithms cannot replicate: creative problem-solving and building strong relationships with other people.

Firms are looking beyond traditional credentials such as a university degree and placing added emphasis on those who can navigate ambiguous scenarios and are fluent in using AI tools, said business leaders during a panel discussion entitled “Will Asia shape the future of AI?” at Asia Future Summit 2026.

While workers with deep expertise in specific fields are still valuable, workers are now expected to be “builders and problem-solvers”, said Temus chief executive Sng Ren Yeong, citing practices such as a willingness to experiment and take initiative to turn ideas into real-world applications.

“The question is how to identify these attributes in today’s system – university education is not a very good signal any more because a lot of knowledge and intelligence is now commoditised,” said Sng.

However, he added that the creativity and resilience that workers show in solving problems and finding ways around ambiguous situations are what deserve attention.

The impact of AI on jobs has become a key point of concern globally.

In Singapore, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has expressed the Government’s worry about the “bottom rung” of the career ladder being broken by AI, and urged employers to be more deliberate in training and mentoring junior hires.

Fellow panellist Aaron Sempf of Amazon Web Services (AWS) said that AI should be used to raise the baseline expectations of workers.

He compared the use of AI with scientific calculators, which students were not allowed to use in the past.

“But my son now does an exam with a scientific calculator – he doesn’t have to learn all the formulae, but the work that he’s tackling is far more complex,” said Sempf, who serves as AWS’ principal for frontier AI in Asia-Pacific and Japan.

He added that traditional hiring formats that quiz candidates on their knowledge are now less important, with organisations such as AWS choosing to test candidates’ problem-solving skills.

“Putting somebody in a difficult or ambiguous scenario and saying ‘solve it’ gives them the opportunity to show their ability to learn or solve their way out of problems,” said Sempf.

While machines excel at computational logic, the panel noted that high-stakes decisions ultimately hinge on human negotiation and sound judgment.

For instance, Trip.com uses AI to help personalise recommendations for travellers, support multilingual customer service around the clock, and generate marketing assets.

However, vital business interactions such as bidding for a new contract cannot be outsourced to AI, said the travel booking platform’s group CEO, Jane Sun.

“You can use AI to empower the worker so that he has good background information on the client – but you can never send it out to negotiate for more,” said Sun, adding that the company is ramping up hiring for roles such as tour guides as travel demand grows.

The emphasis on exclusively human values was mirrored in the banking sector.

Earlier in July, OCBC rolled out AI avatars that can answer customer queries on portfolio performance at any time of the day, and help relationship managers monitor markets in different time zones and understand customer needs better.

Instead of replacing relationship managers, the bank plans to hire 600 additional workers in these roles for its consumer banking business over the next three years.

The relationship managers help to provide the human advice needed as customers become more knowledgeable about their investment portfolios and have higher-level questions they need assistance with, said OCBC group CEO Tan Teck Long.

“It gives us a new way of working where we can actually help the customer better and also help our employees,” said Tan.

Said Sun: “I would really encourage our young people to look at fields that take into account human values, that cannot be replicated and (involve work that) is not purely logical. That’s where humans can still play a very important role.” THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: US chip restrictions could slow AI financing, cloud Singapore banks’ loan growth outlook
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore banks’ loan growth outlook could be clouded by US export controls on advanced artificial intelligence chips, as lenders are likely to scale back the financing of data centres amid heightened uncertainty, analysts said.

While near-term impact is likely “contained” given the Singapore lenders’ conservative approach to data centre financing, greater scrutiny of China-linked exposures could result in a loss of a key growth driver going forward, the analysts noted.

“The banks are assessing how this impacts their lending pipelines, and it’s fair to expect some slowdown in underwriting as there is more scrutiny,” said Jayden Vantarakis, head of Asean equity research at Macquarie Capital. “Any slowdown in loan underwriting would drive lower loan fee income.”

This comes as investors have long been bullish on South-east Asia for powering the supply of physical AI infrastructure for frontier model training.

There will likely be some near-term moderation in financing activity as operators reassess their expansion plans and seek greater clarity on licensing requirements, said Joanna Cheah, Asean research analyst at Jefferies.

Alicia Garcia Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at Natixis Corporate & Investment Banking, noted that banks are already tightening due diligence on end users and compliance amid higher credit scrutiny on China-linked exposures.

Future underwriting will prioritise clear non-China end users, strong sponsors and documented compliance over pure capacity growth, she said.

“The controls extend beyond supply chains into financing, and will slow the boom more than derail it for well-positioned banks,” she said.

This would challenge the banks’ constructive loan-growth outlook for next year, as the lenders cited demand for data centre-related financing as a key driver prior to the latest developments, noted a CreditSights report.

It noted that a shift away from data centre financing towards trade loans and domestic mortgages could also lower margins given that these loans typically carry lower yields.

Small portion of loan book

Nevertheless, impact on the banks is likely contained and should not extend to asset quality or credit shocks, given their diversified loan books, analysts said.

The data centre exposure of Singapore banks is small, at around 3 to 5 per cent of the total loan book for DBS, OCBC and UOB, although CreditSights noted that the figure is higher than global peers’ 1 to 2 per cent.

For Maybank, data centre exposure is also “relatively small”, making up 0.6 per cent of the bank’s total gross loans outstanding as at Sep 30.

But its spokesperson said that it was too early to determine the full impact as the situation continues to evolve, and further clarity was needed on the implementation and scope of the measures.

“It does remove a possible loan growth avenue but we don’t anticipate a significant change to asset quality,” said Lorraine Tan, director of equity research (Asia) at Morningstar.

Jefferies’ Cheah added that data centre financing is not central to her earnings or returns assumptions, given the banks’ diversified loan portfolios, strong capital buffers and rising fee income.

OCBC group CEO Tan Teck Long told The Business Times in an interview on Nov 19 that the bank does not finance companies that are involved in the re-export of high-end chips, and reviews its customers to ensure that they are in line with regulations.

Its data centre financing is mainly related to hyperscaler use, with less than half a per cent of financing in AI-related training, he added.

Elaine Lam, OCBC head of global corporate banking, added that the bank will continue to focus on projects backed by strong sponsors, proven operating capabilities and clear cash flow visibility.

UOB also does not foresee material concerns for now, as the majority of its exposure is to US hyperscalers that are compliant with the new rules, said a spokesperson.

As for DBS, a spokesperson said that the bank has continued to work on data centre financing transactions and remains committed to supporting existing data centre customers, subject to applicable regulatory requirements across jurisdictions.

Citi, HSBC and Standard Chartered declined to comment.

Long-term demand intact

Analysts do not expect the restrictions to fundamentally alter the longer-term structural demand for digital infrastructure across Asean, although the composition of demand and pace of capacity additions could change.

Banks will likely increasingly differentiate financing opportunities based on the ultimate end user and intended use of computing capacity, rather than simply the domicile of the data centre operator, Jefferies’ Cheah said.

This would mean more stringent due diligence, tighter loan covenants, greater scrutiny of underlying off-take agreements and licensing requirements, and potentially higher risk premiums or lower leverage for projects with greater regulatory uncertainty, she added.

OCBC’s Tan also expects the data centre space to continue growing due to supply constraints.

“Because of the severe shortage, if someone vacates one data centre, my personal view is that someone else will take it,” he said. “If one of the hyperscaler wants a data centre somewhere in South-east Asia, and then something becomes available, it’s not a bad (deal for the hyperscaler to take over the space).”

But the CreditSights analysts warned that the US hyperscalers will unlikely relocate a substantial proportion of their Al computing infrastructure from the US to South-east Asia, due to US industrial and national-security policies and operational challenges.

However, US hyperscalers will likely continue to invest in regional cloud and Al infrastructure to serve local customers and meet data-residency requirements, the report said.

On Nov 19, the US tightened export controls on advanced AI chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia to prevent Chinese companies from circumventing licensing requirements through data centres in these markets.

The Financial Times subsequently reported that Nvidia stopped the shipment of its servers to the four Asean nations, although Singapore Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong later commented that the government has not confirmed a shipment halt and is working with local companies to assess operational impacts.

data.title: Issue 222: Asia Pacific’s sustainability disclosure gaps; COP31’s failed talks
data.description:
Sustainability reporting

Time to raise sustainability capability in Asian firms

As the world faces growing climate risks, Asia’s listed companies must not only strengthen their climate governance and strategy, but also assure increasingly discerning stakeholders that they are doing so.

A new analysis by The Business Times and the National University of Singapore’s Centre for Governance and Sustainability finds that while Asia Pacific’s leading companies are mostly meeting the base requirements on sustainability reporting, significant gaps remain in the quality of their disclosures.

The Asia Pacific Sustainability Index (APSI) scores the 50 largest listed companies in 14 regional markets – a total of 700 companies – on six aspects of sustainability reporting.

The findings suggest that the region’s leading companies have reached a baseline standard when it comes to sustainability reporting. For example, almost all the companies identified material environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues and their approach to selecting those issues. Almost all of the companies explain the channels through which they engage with stakeholder groups. Almost all companies report on their Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions, which are emissions directly generated from their operations and indirectly from purchased energy, heating and cooling.

These are encouraging. Some of these standards are relatively easy to achieve, no doubt, but at least the companies are picking the low-hanging fruit instead of ignoring them.

The next challenge for the companies is naturally to reach higher. Now that most of the companies understand how to identify material ESG matters and how to measure their exposure to these issues, they need to ensure that they are able to extend these insights into robust strategies.

The journey should start with ensuring that leadership is equipped and motivated to chart the path ahead. Although 92 per cent of the assessed companies disclose that the board is responsible for sustainability, only 41 per cent describe directors’ sustainability-related skills or competencies, and only 37 per cent reported that board members received sustainability training in the past three years.

Furthermore, while 80 per cent of companies say that management is involved in overseeing material ESG factors, only 55 per cent of companies link top-executive remuneration to sustainability performance, and only 21 per cent disclose the specific weighting of sustainability-related factors in remuneration.

The numbers suggest that many companies’ leadership may shoulder responsibility and oversight of ESG matters on paper, but they are not delivering as well as they should in practice. That is because they are not proficient on such matters, or they are not properly incentivised to produce sustainability-related results.

The APSI study finds more than 80 per cent of companies identify climate-related risks and opportunities, explain their impacts on the business, strategy and financial planning, and describe response strategies. However, only 64 per cent of the companies provided climate-related scenario analysis, and only 28 per cent provided quantitative climate scenario analysis.

The quality of the disclosures is further weakened by poor assurance. In South-east Asia, especially, internal assurance tends to be the norm, with the use of internal assurance significantly surpassing the use of external assurance. For Asia Pacific as a whole, only two-thirds of companies obtain external assurance, most of which is at a limited assurance level as opposed to the more rigorous reasonable assurance threshold.

The result is that many climate strategies are inadequate or lack rigour. For instance, disclosure about physical climate risks is generally lower among companies listed in developing South-east Asia, which ironically is one of the more vulnerable regions in the world to physical climate damage and loss.

Companies will find the need to better address sustainability goes beyond fulfilling regulatory requirements or doing well on sustainability scoring indices.

The world is almost certainly going to fail at limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-Industrial level, which means that greater climate-related turmoil is in the forecast for the years ahead. The insurance industry is already acutely aware that climate-related catastrophes are occurring more frequently and at greater severity. In 2026 alone, the world has experienced heat waves in Europe and parts of Asia, and massive floods in Nepal and Thailand.

More recently, climate negotiators in Turkey for the annual United Nations climate conference known as COP31 failed to reach a deal because countries failed to reach consensus, the first failure since 2009. The war in Iran is disrupting energy supply chains, while artificial intelligence sparks a ravenous need for electricity and water. As a result, climate cooperation is being strained, and climate transition risks are elevated in such a fragmented world.

Companies need to raise their climate capabilities to match the trajectory of the disruption.

Just as importantly, companies need to assure their stakeholders that they are able to weather the figurative and literal storms that lie ahead. This means improving the quality of sustainability disclosures and providing enough details to demonstrate that the company isn’t merely paying lip service to sustainability. As climate-related risks increase, stakeholders will also become more discerning and demanding about which companies are worth supporting.

In a world where everyone is already reporting Scope 1 and 2 emissions, setting decarbonisation targets, giving their directors oversight over sustainability and identifying material issues, a company that merely skims the surface will not stand out. But appoint sustainability experts to the board, provide robust scenario analyses about the business, subject sustainability disclosures to rigorous audits, and tie leadership compensation to sustainability outcomes using meaningful indicators, and a company will set itself apart from the rest of the field.

COP31

Failed talks whisper of fragmented future

Businesses and investors should contend with heightened physical and transition climate risks, as failed climate talks in Turkey suggest that the world remains on a trajectory towards a fragmented climate policy landscape.

Negotiators at the annual United Nations climate conference – this year’s edition is called COP31 – failed to agree on key commitments despite more than two weeks of talks. The major rift centred on fossil fuels, with a major bloc of countries objecting to the final proposal because it did not address the role of fossil fuels in global warming.

The last time that the COP meetings failed to reach a deal was in Copenhagen in 2009.

The incremental impact of the failed COP is probably minor.

Given that previous years’ agreements had mentioned fossil fuels, opponents of the proposed text in Turkey argue that no deal is better than a pact that represents backsliding on a critical aspect of climate change. While COP deals send important signals that help to nudge capital and policy towards priority areas – this year’s would have launched an electrification pledge – the actual translation of deal to action can take a long time, and previous years’ commitments are still in place.

But COP31 represents a new and important data point in understanding where global climate action is headed, and it’s not a great direction.

The Network for Greening the Financial System, an initiative run by central banks and financial-sector regulators, maintains a set of climate scenarios that represent different combinations of physical and transition climate risks. The quadrant where both physical risk and transition risk are high is named “Too Little, Too Late”, and it is in this quadrant where the “Fragmented World” scenario sits.

This scenario assumes a “delayed and divergent climate policy response” among countries globally. In this scenario, countries with net-zero targets only make it 80 per cent of the way there, while other countries stick with current policies. Global warming reaches 2.4 degrees Celsius above pre-Industrial levels. It’s essentially a high-chaos scenario.

The trajectory could yet shift. A large driver of the current strain in international climate cooperation is the Iran war, which has led to countries prioritising the economy and defence above climate action. When and if those pressures ease up, and if climate-related loss and damage become significant enough to shape policy, countries may find themselves pulling in directions that are more aligned than they are now.

In any case, businesses and investors must be prepared for a more turbulent climate policy landscape, with significant variation in rules from market to market. The physical risk landscape could be considerably more uneven as well, with certain areas more exposed to climate-related damage than others on the basis of geography and investments in adaptation and resilience.

But messy situations can also be opportunities. Those that can figure out how to deal with the mess will be well rewarded.

  • Singapore takes ‘prosper thy neighbour’ approach to Asean energy trade: Tan See Leng
  • Singapore unveils green shipping, AI governance initiatives with China after PM Wong meets Premier Li Qiang
  • Boards need to come clean on directors’ sustainability vision

data.title: David Neo, Heng Swee Keat to join 120 Singapore delegates in Kobe for Spotlight Singapore
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Culture, Community and Youth Minister David Neo and Heng Swee Keat, chairman of the National Research Foundation, will be attending the 20th anniversary of Spotlight Singapore in Kobe, Japan, joining 120 delegates from the city-state.

Singapore’s cultural diplomacy platform – which brings together enterprise, arts, culture and people-to-people exchanges – returns to Japan on Tuesday (Dec 1) as the two countries commemorate 60 years of diplomatic relations.

The six-day programme also builds on their recently established strategic partnership.

It was last hosted in Japan in 2006, where the programme was held in Tokyo. Singapore Ambassador to Japan Ong Eng Chuan will welcome the delegation in Kobe.

Neo, who is also second minister for education, will be the event’s guest of honour, while Heng headlines the business conference on Thursday, where he will participate in a fireside chat.

This conference, organised in partnership with The Business Times, brings together leaders from the two countries to discuss innovation, sustainable growth, research commercialisation, healthcare and biotechnology.

It will also build new cross-border partnerships, with Singapore and Japanese partners taking part in a memorandum of understanding signing ceremony.

The speakers and panellists at the conference are:

  • Adjunct Professor Danny Soon, CEO of the Consortium for Clinical Research and Innovation, Singapore, and executive director of the Singapore Clinical Research Institute;
  • Eigo Nosaka, founder, president and CEO of Treasure Factory;
  • Hiroaki Koizumi, founder of Rokusho-sha;
  • Kaoru Asano, senior executive adviser of Sysmex Corp;
  • Dr Sue-Anne Toh, co-founder and CEO of Novi Health;
  • Dr Tsuyoshi Nishiwaki, managing executive officer of Asics Corp; and,
  • Dr Zhou Lihan, co-founder and CEO of Mirxes.

Beyond the conference, the delegates – which comprise business leaders, entrepreneurs, artists, youth and community partners – will attend industry exchanges across biomedical and health technology, advanced manufacturing, lifestyle and creative industries, and circular economy and sustainability.

They will also be presented with various arts and cultural displays, from the unveiling of a friendship mural to traditional dance and music performances.

The Kobe edition of Spotlight Singapore was first announced in June this year, at a launch event attended by BT editor Chen Huifen, TRCL chairperson Jennie Chua, Spotlight Singapore organising committee chairperson Lee Suan Hiang, and Millet Group chairperson Lim Yeong Seng, among others.

TRCL, an arts and culture not-for-profit organisation, manages and organises Spotlight Singapore, while Millet Group supports the platform.

data.title: Malaysia mulls commuter pass as Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone blueprint takes shape
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore residents working in the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) could receive a special pass to ease their cross-border commutes, and details could come in a master blueprint in early 2027.

Malaysia’s Economy Minister Akmal Nasir said the pass is part of a broader push to smooth the cross-border movement of people and goods and to encourage long-term commitment from businesses and workers.

However, he neither specified the benefits the pass nor said whether pass holders would still need a separate work permit.

Asked how many people might qualify and whether eligibility would extend beyond senior executives, he replied: “I think I will let the document speak for itself.”

Originally slated for launch in early December, the unveiling has been postponed to early next year after Malaysia shared the draft with Singapore on the sidelines of a bilateral ministerial meeting two weeks ago.

Akmal said the delay gives time for Singapore’s feedback to be incorporated while both sides fix a date for their respective prime ministers to launch the document jointly, preferably in Johor or Kuala Lumpur.

He was speaking to The Business Times on Friday (Nov 27) on the sidelines of SPH Media’s Asia Future Summit 2026, jointly presented by The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

The annual event gathered policymakers, business leaders and industry specialists; OCBC was the presenting sponsor, Marina Bay Sands was the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services, the official cloud partner.

JS-SEZ pulled in RM88.83 billion (US$21.6 billion) in approved investments between January 2025 and June 2026, with RM40.3 billion of that sum realised.

Akmal said sustaining momentum depends on how quickly approved projects start operating, and that the priority in 2027 is to attract more “queen bee” investors.

Such investors are major, industry-leading anchor investors whose entry into a region or sector attracts a wider ecosystem of suppliers, technology partners and supporting businesses.

He said clustering projects simplifies the provision of utilities and builds business opportunities for suppliers as projects get under way.

He cited Sedenak, a sub-district in Kulai, Johor, as a beneficiary of clustering. It has grown from an agricultural settlement into one of South-east Asia’s fastest-growing data centre and industrial hubs.

Power, water and chips

Malaysia is also preparing legislation that will govern data centres, given that the boom in the industry would test the country’s power and water capacity – even as the US chip curbs create uncertainty over access to advanced processors.

Akmal said the proposed Digital Infrastructure (Data Centres) Bill will clarify investor rules and regulate security, operational resilience and continuity.

Noting that projects involve multiple authorities, including state governments handling the applications for approvals, he added that the government must ensure facilities secure the necessary utilities without disrupting supply to domestic consumers.

The Digital Ministry has told Parliament the Bill would be tabled in 2027.

Asked about the Megaspeed case and US trade restrictions, Akmal said there are still a lot of uncertainties and Malaysia’s Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry would lead talks with its counterparts.

He cited Google’s investment in Malaysia as an example of the questions that could arise over how projects would proceed if chip supplies were constrained.

“Things can change within a month, or less than a month,” he said, adding that his ministry’s job was to set the long-term direction while trade officials handle the negotiations.

Increase minimum wage

Turning to the wider economy, Akmal said Malaysia’s third-quarter growth of 5.5 per cent had exceeded his expectations.

He pointed to consumer spending and manufacturing, and said businesses were putting some capital into machinery and other investments, and into funding day-to-day operations.

Asked why workers say they see little improvement in their salaries and living costs, he said productivity was rising faster than wages.

Akmal noted that the government had agreed to review the minimum wage in 2027, and is exploring ways to bring graduate pay to around RM2,500.

He raised wage compression as a concern, saying semi-skilled workers and graduates could see little benefit from a higher minimum wage.

“Growth will just be considered as a number if the population cannot feel it,” he said.

Akmal pointed to the 13th Malaysia Plan’s target of raising employees’ compensation to 40 per cent of gross domestic product.

He said higher-value work, such as advanced semiconductor packaging and integrated circuit design, could help translate demand for more specialised skills into higher pay.

Earlier, Bank Negara Malaysia revealed that employees’ compensation stood at 33.9 per cent of GDP, below the 40 per cent target under the 13th Malaysia Plan.

Keeping policy on track

Asked whether Malaysia’s economic agenda could survive a Cabinet reshuffle ahead of a possible 2027 general election, Akmal said he had built upon existing policies when taking over the ministry.

“It’s OK to carry forward the good progress that we make,” he said, noting that Forum Ekonomi Malaysia – the ministry’s first event next year, slated for January – will focus on the country’s economic issues.

Calling the five-year 13th Malaysia Plan a “guardrail” for economic direction, he cited the National Semiconductor Strategy, National Energy Transition Roadmap and New Industrial Master Plan as multi-term commitments.

He pointed to carbon capture as an example, noting Malaysia has set up a regulator and identified four projects under its carbon capture, utilisation and storage road map – the kind of initiatives he expects to endure across leadership changes.

Political activity will likely intensify ahead of next year’s expected general election, he said, but added that “the economic focus must remain there”.

data.title: Asean must counter economic nationalism with deeper integration, wider partnerships: DPM Gan
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Asean must counter rising economic nationalism with deeper integration and wider partnerships, in a world where governments are placing more emphasis on self-reliance and control over critical industries, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong on Nov 27.

“Raising barriers among ourselves would narrow the opportunities available to each of us,” he said. A more integrated Asean would strengthen its value as a partner, while broader tie-ups open up more opportunities for the region.

Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), was delivering a keynote speech at SPH Media’s Asia Future Summit 2026, jointly presented by The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

The annual event gathered policymakers, business leaders and industry experts, with OCBC as the presenting sponsor, Marina Bay Sands as the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services as the official cloud partner.

In his speech, Gan identified three factors that make integration and partnerships especially important: artificial intelligence, geopolitical shocks and geo-economic contestation. “Each can strengthen the impulse to turn inward. Yet each also makes cooperation more crucial,” he said.

His remarks followed the United States’ announcements of fresh tariffs and chip export restrictions over the past two weeks, moves which affected many in South-east Asia as the region finds itself in the crosshairs of sharpening rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

“Geo-economic competition is reshaping the networks through which we trade, invest and access technology,” Gan said, with governments paying closer attention to dependencies and control over critical capabilities.

“Asean countries cannot determine how major powers manage their differences,” he added. “But we can maintain relationships across these divides and remain a bridge for trade, investment and cooperation.”

Doing so would require that Asean earn and sustain its partners’ confidence in the grouping’s integrity, institutional reliability and business environment by issuing clear and predictable rules, upholding its laws and commitments, and taking firm action against wrongdoing, he said.

“As scrutiny of international trade and investment intensifies, maintaining these standards becomes even more important,” he added.

ASEAN will mark its 60th anniversary in 2027, with Singapore pushing for deeper integration and wider partnerships as it takes on Asean’s rotating chairmanship at a time of heightened geopolitical contestation.

Both the US and China would continue to be key economic partners for Asean, Gan said, with their businesses, technologies and markets important to the region’s growth.

Both countries are among the region’s largest trading partners and sources of foreign direct investment.

In tandem, the grouping is strengthening tie-ups with other partners that would expand the region’s economic options and reduce its exposure to disruptions, Gan said.

These include negotiations to upgrade Asean’s trade agreements with South Korea and Canada, moves to expand and enhance the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and growing links with other regional groupings such as the European Union and Gulf Cooperation Council.

Asean is also strengthening integration within the grouping, with Gan highlighting recent efforts that would help firms better tap suppliers and customers within the region.

A recently upgraded Asean Trade in Goods Agreement, set to be rolled out in end-2026, will help businesses reduce costs through streamlined procedures and more transparent rules, he said, while a customs-related mutual recognition arrangement would give trusted traders faster clearances and priority treatment in participating countries.

And a regional Digital Economy Framework Agreement signed earlier in the month would make cross-border transactions, payments and access to digital services easier, he added.

These would make Asean more valuable as a place to produce and market to serve, and form a stronger regional base enabling the grouping to “engage the world with greater confidence”, Gan said. THE STRAITS TIMES

  • For more information, visit www.asiafuturesummit.com

data.title: Data centre giants in Singapore play down double whammy of US chip curbs, reported Nvidia shipment freeze
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] US data centre giants Equinix and Digital Realty are playing down the fallout from Nvidia’s reported suspension of artificial intelligence server shipments to South-east Asia, even as analysts warn of project delays, higher compliance costs and more cautious lending.

While analysts expect the reported Nvidia chip ban affecting Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia to be temporary, it adds to the uncertainty facing a region already grappling with tighter US semiconductor controls announced on Nov 16, aimed at curbing China’s access to advanced chips.

Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said on Friday (Nov 27) that Singapore has not confirmed the shipment halt, first reported by the Financial Times.

“Our confidence in South-east Asia is unchanged,” an Equinix spokesperson told The Business Times, pointing to broad-based demand from enterprises, cloud and network providers, and financial services firms.

Its customers continue to plan for long-term growth, and the company continues to invest across Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines, the spokesperson said.

Equinix noted that as a colocation provider, it does not directly provide access to computing power, including advanced graphics processing units.

Digital Realty, meanwhile, expects limited impact on its existing business, given that its South-east Asian operations primarily serve cloud and enterprise customers through colocation services.

It is reviewing the latest US export controls to assess their implications, including licensing and reporting requirements.

Other data centre players operating here – including Keppel, ST Telemedia Global Data Centres, Singtel and AirTrunk – declined to comment. Nvidia has yet to respond to queries.

Shipment freeze could delay projects

Analysts expect Nvidia’s reported shipment suspension to be temporary, although it could disrupt project timelines and financing as uncertainties remain.

Paul Chew, head of research at Phillip Securities Research, views the suspension as “precautions against all the new (US) regulations”.

Meanwhile, Andrew Kitson, head of technology industry research at BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, expects Nvidia to “move quickly to secure workarounds to minimise disruptions to these markets” where possible.

With chief executive Jensen Huang back at the helm, there is a possibility that export controls “may not be implemented in full and that some exemptions may be made”, he said, citing Huang’s influence with the Trump administration and Nvidia’s push for greater access to China.

Alicia Garcia Herrero, Asia-Pacific chief economist at Natixis Corporate & Investment Banking, said the suspension risks delaying AI server deliveries and stalling projects tied to Chinese customers, with financing already put on hold for some deals.

“Most vulnerable are China-linked operators, neoclouds serving Chinese AI firms, and markets with high Chinese exposure such as Malaysia (Johor) and Thailand,” she said. “Singapore is relatively less exposed due to its more diversified customer base.”

This comes as the latest US export controls extend restrictions beyond physical chip shipments to Chinese companies’ remote access to advanced computing power, with implications for data centres across the region.

In an earlier report, Natixis estimated that nearly a third of operational data centre capacity across the four affected South-east Asian markets is linked to Chinese ownership or tenants, with the proportion exceeding 45 per cent in both Malaysia and Thailand.

Joanna Cheah, Asean research analyst, Jefferies, said that Singapore’s relatively stringent approach to regulatory compliance also leaves its data centre sector “better positioned” to navigate the new US restrictions.

The impact could be more pronounced in regional markets where a larger share of new data centre capacity is being built to cater to Chinese AI-related demand, she added.

Investment outlook grows murkier

Even if Nvidia’s reported chip ban gets resolved, analysts still expect South-east Asia’s data centre investment expansion to take a hit from tighter US export controls.

“Combined, they are likely to slow and make more selective the region’s AI data centre investment boom by raising compliance costs, licensing uncertainty and risks for China-facing projects,” said Garcia Herrero.

She noted that capital will likely gravitate towards facilities with secure access to chips and diversified customer bases, particularly those serving US and other Western companies.

Similarly, Phillip Securities’ Chew said that regional demand will taper as financing becomes more cautious and Chinese demand weakens, even as it becomes increasingly concentrated among US hyperscalers.

However, BMI’s Kitson expects global hyperscalers’ appetite for expansion and investment to cool over the next 12 to 18 months as companies assess how the new semiconductor trade rules are implemented and enforced.

While South-east Asia’s digital transformation will sustain demand for data centre services, he cautioned that local demand may not immediately compensate for a shortfall in Chinese demand.

Uncertainties persist, even as countries such as Singapore have said they are studying the details and engaging with the US authorities on the measures.

Kitson also pointed to Donald Trump’s earlier threat to impose tariffs on US-based hyperscalers developing AI data centres outside the US.

“How this might be enforced – even if the tech companies did not push back and allow this to happen – is far from clear,” he added.

Additional reporting by Young Zhan Heng
